title: One Yardstick for Five Robots: Reach Volume by Sampling, the Room a Robot Takes for It, and What the Numbers Do and Do Not Say

questions.question: Why ask every robot the same question?
options: So that the fastest robot is found
Their reaches are described in different terms and cannot be compared otherwise
Because each maker measures reach in its own units
To make the test code shorter
questions.explanation: Joint ranges, leg strokes and travels are not comparable. Whether the tool can be put at a point, level, is something every robot can answer.

questions.question: How was the volume found?
options: From each maker's data sheet
By a formula for each family's shape
By asking the question at random points and counting the yes answers
By slicing the reach into layers and adding their areas
questions.explanation: The shapes have no formula. 40000 random points in a box, and the share that can be reached times the box's volume is the estimate.

questions.question: Which had the largest reach volume?
options: The gantry, whose box is all usable
The six axis arm, 1.731 m3
The SCARA, at 0.084 m3
The delta, at 0.072 m3
questions.explanation: The arm's reach is most of a ball. The SCARA's is a slab 0.15 m thick, because a flat table is its job.

questions.question: The Stewart platform used what share of its room?
questions.explanation: Its base and legs take up far more room than the small volume its platform moves in.

questions.question: Does the largest volume make the best robot?
options: No: volume leaves out speed, payload, stiffness, accuracy and the shape of the work
Yes, for any task that fits inside it
Yes, since reach is what a robot is bought for
Only when two robots have the same payload
questions.explanation: The arm's volume was twenty times the SCARA's and most of it is no use to a table job. The task decides what counts.

questions.question: Why is the standard error of use?
options: It corrects the estimate's bias
It makes the random points repeatable
It gives the volume's exact value in the limit
It says how many points the estimate needs and is the square root of n small
questions.explanation: It shrinks as the square root of the number of points, so it says what an estimate is worth: about 0.4 percent for the SCARA at 40000 points.
